Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
items.summary: Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests. Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. The Advantage of Catching JiTTests Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests. How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points. A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”). Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests. To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch. How It Works The entire system workflow happens in five stages: Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions. Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them. At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent. Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent). Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches. Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment) Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive). The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review: The weak-catch test-case code. The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace). The code changes between parent and child (the diff). The inferred diff intent. Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake) We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake). LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration. Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out) Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers. Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output. Table 2. Operational differences between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop approaches. The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results. As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives. In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe. Figure 2. The impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta in the first half of 2026. Why It Matters Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended. The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item. Read the Paper Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure. The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
items.summary: With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron crawler and we’re trying to learn a bit about game development along the way. However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we wanted to get a narrator and voice over. But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which uses voice embeddings for custom voices. With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it. What Qwen Offers Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We initially used Kokoro. However Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique. In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models: 1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio 1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions 1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model. At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone. Playing With It For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI Conf, cut between two pauses so that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper. The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original recording. Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother. The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used 0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too: import torch from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa") design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw) wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design( text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), language="English", instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking " "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading " "aloud to a friend.", ) You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together: Interactive demo: see the post on the website. Voice Embeddings What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below). Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices: base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw) def fingerprint(path): prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True) return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding def blend(a, b, t): a, b = a.float(), b.float() mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to( torch.bfloat16 ) armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac") Here is the same sentence in eleven blends: Interactive demo: see the post on the website. Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice. If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference: import soundfile as sf mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5) audio, rate = say( open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed ) # say() is shown further down sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate) final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac") The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file. So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good does that work? I took an episode of State of Agentic Coding, the podcast Ben and I record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an embedding of me form the conference. Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right. On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For instance ECAPA, finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows. Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches: Interactive demo: see the post on the website. Instructed Cloned Voices But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either (voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers: cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw) def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"): ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)]) told = [ cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0] if instruct else None ] voice = { "ref_code": [None], "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec], "x_vector_only_mode": [True], "icl_mode": [False], } codes, _ = cv.model.generate( input_ids=ids, instruct_ids=told, voice_clone_prompt=voice, languages=[language], non_streaming_mode=True, **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7), ) wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}]) return wavs[0], rate wav, rate = say( "I really thought this would work.", armin, "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.", ) Pick a speaker for the slot, a model and an instruction: Interactive demo: see the post on the website. Instructions work on cloned voices, but less reliably than on the built-in speakers, and it depends on the emotion, but honestly, it came out better than I anticipated. Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their game. Other Fun Math If a voice is a point in a 2048-dimensional space and blending works we can maybe do some other funny math on it. The obvious one is to try to see if some math can be used to manipulate gender. To find it I had VoiceDesign create 14 different voices for men and women each. When you then take the average woman minus the average man you can then move any voice along that direction: women = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/f{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float() men = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/m{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float() middle = (women.mean(0) + men.mean(0)) / 2 axis = women.mean(0) - men.mean(0) axis = axis / axis.norm() def move(xvec, t): """Put the voice at position t along the gender axis, keep the rest.""" x = xvec.float() return (x + (t - (x - middle) @ axis) * axis).to(torch.bfloat16) Here is the result for my clone: Interactive demo: see the post on the website. Anyways, that’s that. If you want to play around with Qwen3 TTS I hope this was of some help, and maybe you got some ideas of what to do with the voice embeddings. Use it for good, not evil.

items.summary: Amp now has a Mac: ask it to work on your iOS or Mac app and watch it build, test, and run the app. Port to iPhone Duo New Mac App Feature Penny runs on iPhone 17 Pro. Amp has it open in DeviceHub on a Mac next to the thread. Amp checks Penny on the iPhone Duo and fixes the layout for both screens. Then it opens the new build on the Duo, closed. Amp unfolds the Duo, and Penny switches to the side-by-side layout. It taps a transaction to open it. Amp's report: what it checked on the Duo. Amp recorded the Mac while it checked: closed, unfolded, tapped. Amp runs the iPod app for the Mac as it is today. Amp adds a Model setting for the black and red U2 iPod. Then it drives the app: Settings, Model, U2. Music, Artists, scroll to The Avalanches. The Avalanches, “Since I Left You.” Now playing on the U2 iPod. Amp's report: what it built and how it checked it. Amp recorded the Mac while it played the song itself. How It Works Your thread still runs on a Linux orb, next to your dev server and toolchain. The Mac is a second machine attached to that orb. Amp can automatically start a Mac, run commands on it, and read and write files, so it decides on its own when the work needs a Mac. When it does, our server boots a fresh Mac in the cloud with Xcode and the simulators installed, in about 30 seconds. Your orb connects to it and keeps your code in sync, so Amp still edits on the orb and only builds, runs, and tests on the Mac. Screenshots, logs, and builds come back to the thread, and the app on the Mac reaches your backend on the orb through portals. The thread's Mac tab streams the Mac's screen. Watch Amp's work, or take control of the Mac and try the app yourself. Every Mac starts fresh, and nothing on it is saved. When Amp is done with a Mac, it keeps it running for 20 more minutes. If you send a follow-up in that time, Amp reuses the same Mac and its build cache instead of starting a new Mac and building from scratch. After that, the Mac is deleted. To delete it right away, archive the thread or ask Amp to stop the Mac. Morbs Are Dead, Long Live macOS Satellites Before shipping macOS Satellites, we tried out Morbs: orbs that ran the whole thread on a Mac. But we ran into issues that made the approach unfeasible for a wider rollout. Docker and your backend took minutes to start there,[^1] and keeping a Mac disk around for every thread got expensive. So we split the thread across two machines. Everything that runs well on Linux stays on the orb and starts fast, and a Mac only shows up for the work that needs macOS.[^2] We're calling them macOS Satellites because they orbit your orb. 如何在“不能出错”的系统里使用 AI Coding？分布式存储实践与边界
items.summary: AI 能让代码写得更快，但在「不能出错」的分布式存储系统里，如何确保提效不变成风险？本文结合美团基础技术部在 AI 评审、问题排查和自动化开发中的真实实践，分享 AI 能帮上什么忙、容易在哪些地方犯错，以及哪些地方仍需要人来把关。比「多写代码」更重要的，是让代码和结论经得起验证。希望这些经验能为复杂系统中的 AI 应用提供参考，在享受效率提升的同时，守住质量与稳定性的底线。 1. 背景：为什么分布式存储需要更审慎地使用 AI Coding 今年年初以来，随着Agent的普及，AI Coding 在功能开发、测试生成、脚本编写和执行、问题排查这些场景里都已经用得上了：读代码更快，实现和测试可以先让它写一版，研发之外的一部分杂活也能交给它去跑。 效率上去了，质量上的账也要重新算。同样的人力，一个版本里能交付的功能更多，改动的代码也更多，就算 AI 写的代码千行缺陷率和人写的持平，一个版本累计引入的缺陷绝对数量照样会涨。所以 AI Coding 的目标不能只是更快地写代码，提速的同时，代码质量和验证充分性还得比常规研发要求得更高。 分布式存储把这个问题放大了。代码规模大，模块之间关系复杂，一致性、并发、持久化、故障恢复和性能每一项都碰得到。一处看上去很局部的改动，平时可能一切正常，等到节点重启、磁盘异常、网络抖动或者高并发的时候才暴露出来。出了问题，受影响的也不会只是某一个功能，而是上层业务的数据可用性和系统稳定性，严重时还会波及数据正确性。存储服务支撑着大量上层业务，故障影响面大，修复也困难，对缺陷的容忍度极低。 要满足这样的质量要求，光让 AI 生成代码不够，AI 评审（Code Review）、AI 测试与验证、AI Debug 和受控自动化也得一起建起来，AI 生成的代码才能放心地进入研发流程。本文结合存储团队在 AI 评审、AI Debug 和 AI 自动化上的实践，讨论在分布式存储这类复杂度高、容错低的系统里，怎样一边用 AI 提速，一边靠更严格的评审、测试、调试和自动化验证守住稳定性与数据正确性，希望对其他类似系统落地 AI Coding 也有参考价值。 2. AI 评审（Code Review）：有益补充，但不能替代人对设计背景的判断 2.1 AI 评审擅长的地方 1. 能注意到跨文件一致性 例：ENABLE_UNITTEST 在三处调用点控制测试 mock 变体的编译分支，但 CMake 迁移把这个名字换成了 WITH_UNITTEST，旧名字再也没被赋过值。单看任何一个文件都挑不出毛病，这个 bug 只存在于文件和文件之间的落差里。 2. 能构造可执行证据 例：AI 指出“这里没做边界检查”之后没有停下，接着构造了一个声明 1 GiB 数值、实际包体只有 5 字节的畸形包，打到真实的解码入口，把崩溃现场抓了出来。 3. 会承认自己证明不了的部分 例：一处疑似的并发竞态，AI 只能靠代码走读找到可疑路径。它明确说，要证实这段交错时序需要 ThreadSanitizer，而当前的工具链跑不了，于是把这条标成“未验证”，没有直接定性为缺陷。 4. AI 对一些常见竞态问题识别率高 例：一处“先读校验、再写推进”、中间没有互斥的更新，多次评审都稳定地识别了出来，给出的修复方向也一致（合并成单个原子操作）。这类常见的并发模式识别得很稳，可以固化成固定检查项。 5. AI 不会漏掉 PR 中被删掉的代码 例：一次重构把某个接口合并成单次 RPC，顺手删掉了成功后清理本地缓存的旧逻辑。AI 指出这会留下一个短暂的时间窗口，期间可能读到过期的旧数据。而人对被删掉的行，本来就最不敏感。 6. AI 会结合存量代码评审增量改动 例：评审之前，AI 会先分析存量代码。改动较大的 PR 里，新代码可能顺手修掉了一个原有问题，人工评审容易把这种顺带修复当成新问题反馈；AI 则会把“原本就有、这次已顺手修掉”的问题单独列出来，并声明不作为问题上报。 7. AI 评审不会局限于代码层面的变更 例：某个 PR 里，三个仓库的构建文件互相用 feature 分支名引用对方，没有固定版本，合入顺序不对或者分支被清理，主干构建就断了。这属于“合并编排”层面的问题，只看 PR 页面的人恰好最容易漏掉，而 AI 把构建文件也当成了评审对象。 2.2 AI 评审容易出错的地方 AI 的误判多数是因为看不到代码之外的东西，比如运维流程、设计决策和团队约定。我们的实践中也看到了AI 评审在修复建议、信噪比、定级和证据取舍上的问题。 1. 代码可达 ≠ 运维可达 例：报告把一处过期 epoch 的代码路径标成了现实风险。人工复核时没有质疑这段代码本身，质疑的是周围的系统到底会不会产生走到这个分支的输入："EPOCH_NOT_MATCH 只会在迁移分裂+1，分裂之后老的region就不存在了，迁移之后再迁移，src也不存在了，所以 EPOCH_NOT_MATCH 理论上走不到这个分支。" 同样的情况也出现在被报告标成竞态窗口的一天过期时间的问题上：“迁移是人工操作，线上不会存在迁移发起一天还没有成功的，需要人工介入，一天的过期时间就是解决这个问题的”。AI 能建模那个计时器，建模不了包在它外面的人工流程。 2. 把和一般实践不同的有意为之当成了缺陷 例：报告把在生产环境里直接调用 abort() 的一致性检查标成了正确性风险，建议改成记录 Error 日志，不要崩溃。实际我们选择了abort，因为存储系统是正确性高于可用性的，在特定场景下，我们宁可 abort，也不能让这个请求继续而产生非常难处理的脏数据。 3. AI 评审附带的修复建议，本身也需要评审 例：AI 针对一个 32 位溢出给出的修复，是校验声明的 size 和实际收到的字节数是否一致。复核时发现 get_size() 返回的是 int，size 落在 2³¹ 到 2³² 之间会被截断成负数，这条校验本身就会静默失效。个例修好了，同一类问题并没有修好。 4. 廉价的“请确认”条目挤占了真正的信号 例：AI 评审把线程池默认值、重命名的配置项、被移除的二级缓存刷新开关都标成了“待确认”。每一条最后得到的回复，依据的都是团队自己压测得出的历史数据，和代码缺陷无关："根据压测调整的，后台线程数调低是为了降低对前台的影响。" 5. AI 评审的问题定级失真 AI 缺少一道界限明确的质量门槛：同一类理论上可能的问题，这次被标成最高级，下次又可能被标成不重要。拿到一份 AI 报告，定级没法完全信，为了保险只能把所有问题挨个审一遍，反而很难聚焦到真正高等级的问题上。 6. 把注释、头文件断言和设计文档当作证据 例：两份 AI 评审用的是同一个“场景 × 约束”框架，却给出了相反的结论。一份直接复述头文件里的断言判定实现是对的；另一份去核对了具体的实现，判定是错的。另一个例子是简单依赖设计文档，即迁移设计文档中要求的版本连续性校验，在代码里却没有任何引用。 两份评审看的代码没有区别，区别在于有没有去验证这些“说明”本身。 2.3 让评审结论可执行：构建测试、集成测试与运行时日志 静态评审只能说明“代码里存在这条路径”。这条路径是否真的会出错、已有的保护能不能拦住、线上有没有发生过，还需要另外三类证据来回答。 2.3.1 构建与单测：把推理变成红绿 实验：AI对一个项目全仓评审的 117 个疑似问题，逐条写 gtest 验证，测试在 master 上失败即视为确认。结果：36 条红测试确认，3 条被证伪（误报），41 条只能靠源码确认，37 条未验证。 判决确定。变红的测试集中在三类：输入触发 abort、错误被吞掉后仍然报成功、解码越界。严重度按失败现象来定就行，不用再看 AI 的措辞。 能证伪。有 3 条发现被测试推翻了，这是静态评审很难给出的结论。 能暴露 CI 自身的问题。比如测试报告里硬编码了 failures="0"，失败用例也不进汇总，所以要让 AI 自己构建、看原始输出，不能只信 CI 的绿灯。 边界。竞态和 UAF 需要 sanitizer，时序问题需要调度控制，故障注入点、受限主机、时钟偏移这些条件也还有缺口，“未验证”那份清单其实就是测试基础设施要补的课。变红的测试也只能证明代码会出错，证明不了线上会产生那个输入：有一个数据迁移场景，测试确认会有数据过期问题，人工复核后发现，在人工操作的流程里，这个过期恰恰是有意设计的。 2.3.2 贴近运行时的集成测试：主要价值是降误报 比如我们有一个项目的类实现做了特殊考虑，使得我们可以在单进程里就拉起真实的 Raft 多节点集群，全仓验证所有需要“生产集群”的场景。 让已有保护参与验证。一个 AI 发现的问题称 leader 切换会导致删除丢数据，而已有的一条集成测试恰好在删除窗口切主，结果证明是安全的。 裁决分歧。比如“快照能否捕获 split 中间态”，两次 AI 评审的意见相反，走真实的 change_peer 入口、加同步点注入写一个测试，就能直接判定。 fake/mock 的边界就是验证的边界。fake 要走真实入口、用生产配置，并写明替换了什么。 例：分布式 KV 的 hang 告警 Bug 没被测出来，是因为测试用的设置和实际生产发生的不同；网络阶段的丢弃保护在单测里被手工喂了时间戳，线上路径却从来不设置。 2.3.3 运行时日志：从“可能发生”到“已经发生” 实验：把一台存储节点 11 天的 WARN 日志（67.8 万行、34 个调用点）交给 AI 映射回源码，找到 5 个缺陷，对应的同学人工确认全部属实，没有误报。 发现静态审查不会怀疑的问题。例：“fail times 1”11 天只出现一次，说明计数器卡住了，hang 告警永远不会触发。 证伪错误假设。例：一个长达 19 分钟的响应，各阶段耗时之和与总耗时的比值恒为 1.0，由此排除了时钟错误，进而定位到发送阶段缺少丢弃保护。 让定级有依据。例：实测阶段耗时已经达到 1,156 秒，离存储这个耗时的 int32 溢出已经不到 2 倍。 其中两个缺陷并不是日志直接触发的，而是 AI 为了解释日志去读相邻代码时发现的，同样属实，日志提供的真实配置和数量级，可能也让相邻代码的推理更准。这只是一个样本，不能说明总能零误报，但足以支持一个做法：能拿到运行时日志时，评审和 Debug 都应附上。日志的局限是只覆盖执行过的路径，行号也可能与部署版本不符（需按消息文本定位）。 2.3.4 小结 证据 | 能回答 | 回答不了 |

items.title: Same Brain, Different Bill
items.summary: Coding benchmarks are mostly about which frontier model solves the most tasks. Now that tokens are no longer free, what it costs to solve them matters just as much. Between the model and the bill sits the harness, which decides what goes into each request and how many requests a task takes. To see how much that layer matters, we gave five open harnesses (goose, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Hermes Agent and pi) the same model, gpt-6.1-sol at high reasoning effort, and the same Terminal-Bench 4 tasks. Each harness attempted every task five times, for 310 scored trials per harness. Results​ goose matched Codex CLI, OpenCode and Hermes Agent on pass rate. Its cost per task was 15 to 43% lower. pi tied goose on both. All five landed within about six points of each other on pass rate, and none differed from goose at 95% confidence. With the same model underneath, no harness solved noticeably more tasks. Cost is a different story. Compared task by task, Codex cost 31% more than goose, OpenCode 18% more and Hermes Agent 75% more, all significant at 95%. pi cost about the same as goose. items.title: Why it’s time to fight AI with AI
items.summary: **Update:** The original $1M Deep Scan campaign has ended. Run your first deep scan for free. First-time users of CodeRabbit Secure with 2+ subscription seats in their organization get up to $1,000 in credits towards their first Deep Scan. [Run Free Deep Scan](https://app.coderabbit.ai/security). A service can run for years with passing tests, patched dependencies, and scans on every pull request while an application-specific vulnerability remains undetected. Read the code function by function and nothing looks dangerous. The vulnerability only shows up when a developer traces the whole workflow and asks what the code assumes along the way. An attacker can ask that question too, and no longer needs to know the codebase to answer it. AI reads unfamiliar code, traces each path through a workflow, and probes the assumptions its authors made, faster than any team of reviewers could. Code that has run untouched for years is now within reach of anyone who points a model at it. That is why we built [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#understand-deep-scan) in [CodeRabbit Secure](https://www.coderabbit.ai/security). It investigates committed code, independently verifies what it finds, and gives developers evidence they can inspect before deciding what to change. [CodeRabbit Secure launch video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pNsZBxzmxF4 "CodeRabbit Secure launch video") ## Attackers got an upgrade Application security has always depended partly on how much time and expertise someone could spend investigating a system. Tracing a request across unfamiliar code takes effort. So does identifying a missing safeguard and working out whether the surrounding application makes it exploitable. AI can now do most of that work. In November 2025, Anthropic [published a report](https://www.anthropic.com/news/disrupting-AI-espionage) on an AI-orchestrated espionage campaign in which AI performed 80% to 90% of the tactical work, with human operators stepping in at only a handful of decision points. The attackers targeted roughly 30 organizations and got into a small number of them. The same AI that finds the vulnerability for an attacker can find it for your team first. You can revisit a service whose original authors have long since moved on, trace the assumptions the code was built on, and add the missing control before anyone else gets there. In an agentic SDLC, ownership of old code can’t sit with security alone; engineering shares it. Animation showing that security is now a shared responsibility between engineering and security teams ## When the flaw is in the application logic Existing scanners do useful work. - Static analysis can follow data across functions and identify unsafe flows - Dependency tools identify known vulnerable packages - Secret scanners look for exposed credentials Keep the tools that cover those jobs. [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#run-a-deep-scan) adds an independent reasoning layer for application-specific flaws that may not match a known rule, vulnerable package, or exposed secret. Animation unwrapping the layers of security scanning, from static analysis and dependency and secret scanning to the reasoning layer Deep Scan adds You can write rules for particular authorization patterns. Mature analysis tools can also model frameworks and trace complex flows. The difficulty sits in expressing every application-specific obligation in advance, especially when a workflow spreads that obligation across several components. [Deep Scan's semantic analysis](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#understand-deep-scan) works out what the application is supposed to enforce, then looks for evidence in the implementation that supports or contradicts the hypothesis. Deep Scan doesn’t stop at the evidence. It checks whether the control is actually missing and what an attacker could do without it. ## Follow one vulnerability across the application Consider this simplified, illustrative refund workflow. Assume the route already authenticates the caller, checks their permission to refund the payment, and accepts only positive amounts in integer minor units. Its handler then does this: ```js async function requestRefund(paymentId, amount) { const payment = await payments.get(paymentId); if (amount > payment.capturedAmount) { throw new Error("Refund exceeds payment"); } return refundJobs.enqueue({ paymentId, amount }); } ``` A worker takes each job and sends the refund request to the payment provider. The application stores prior refunds elsewhere for reconciliation. The amount check looks reasonable in isolation. A customer paid $100, so a request to refund $60 passes. A second request for $60 also passes. Each request satisfies the condition in the handler, but together, they exceed the captured amount. Spotting the comparison is easy. Establishing that the workflow can over-refund takes more work. - Does the worker read the refund history? - Does it reserve funds before contacting the provider? - Does the provider itself enforce a cumulative limit? - Could the second request actually complete? If the provider refuses any refund exceeding the remaining balance, this example does not establish a successful over-refund. Reporting one anyway would ignore a protection on the execution path. Likewise, an accounting function that atomically reserves the refundable balance could invalidate the hypothesis even if the handler never checks it directly. Ruling those out means **connecting the entry point to the job, the worker, and the operation** that moves money. It must account for existing refunds and relevant protections along that path. Only then can you say which sequence of requests violates the application's constraint and under what conditions. That work matters because a useful report lets the developer inspect the path, understand the missing safeguard, and challenge the conclusion. ## Inside a Deep Scan [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/steer-scans) reads the committed codebase, not just the lines changed in a pull request. A suspicious operation means little without the code that determines who can reach it and which protections apply. High-level animation of a Deep Scan mapping the attack surface, hunting for vulnerabilities, verifying findings, and fixing them ### Establish context before deciding what is vulnerable [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#run-a-deep-scan) examines security-relevant parts of the repository, including entry points, trust boundaries, access controls, sensitive operations, and security configuration. This gives the investigation a map of where input enters and where decisions about access are made. [Linked repositories](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/knowledge-base/multi-repo-analysis#use-linked-context-in-deep-scan) can supply read-only context for Deep Scan to investigate and verify findings in the repository being scanned. When a finding cites a linked source, its details show the repository, file, commit, and source link. ![Isometric map of a repository with an orange entry point, a glowing access control block among the modules, and a dashed arrow carrying context in from a smaller linked repo](/content/assets/fighting-ai-with-ai/context-map.png) ### Investigate a hypothesis against the code A useful hypothesis has to be specific enough to test. [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#understand-deep-scan) follows the relevant paths and gathers the code behind a candidate finding. Its explanation must point back to that evidence. Function names, comments, and architectural descriptions can orient the investigation, but they cannot prove that a safeguard executes. ![Isometric map of a codebase where a path runs past a requireAuth comment labeled orients only, through a block labeled executes, to an orange hypothesis block that points at a stack of evidence](/content/assets/fighting-ai-with-ai/hypothesis-evidence.png) ### Challenge the finding independently Writing code and attacking it are different kinds of work. A coding agent’s job is to get a requested change working, not to ask how that change could be abused. Security review exists to ask exactly that, and to back its answer with evidence. CodeRabbit’s **security review is independent of the agent that wrote the code**. Both roles use AI, but they aren’t working toward the same goal. A **separate verifier** checks reachability, existing safeguards, and the conditions required for exploitation. It rejects candidates that overlook protections or rely on unsupported assumptions. Each published finding carries a reachability and exploitability grade, so the list is ranked by what an attacker could actually reach rather than by what a pattern matched. ![Isometric scene of a coding agent crane placing blocks inside a codebase while a separate orange security review tower outside shines a light on one block and produces an evidence panel](/content/assets/fighting-ai-with-ai/independent-challenge.png) Independent verification also has limits. A second model is still a model, and it can repeat the same wrong assumption as the first. Evidence therefore has to remain visible to the developer, who can bring deployment knowledge, business constraints, and external-service behavior that the scan may not establish from available sources. ### Preserve uncertainty Digging deeper into the codebase can reveal an overlooked protection, but it can also extend the chain of assumptions. The deeper the dig, the more important it is to show which code supports the claim, how the pieces connect, and where the evidence ends. Code can show that an operation is reachable without establishing every condition needed to exploit it. An external service, deployment setting, or unavailable component can leave a material question unanswered. When the evidence is incomplete, the finding should say so. ![Isometric map where a traced path reaches an orange block labeled reachable, a marker shows where the evidence ends, and a dashed outline of an external component with a question mark sits outside the codebase](/content/assets/fighting-ai-with-ai/preserve-uncertainty.png) The same principle applies to coverage. The [Attack Surface Map](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/attack-surface) marks each point as fully verified, unverified, or stale. Those statuses show developers which security-relevant areas have current evidence and which still need attention. A fully verified point records an assessment, but it does not guarantee that the code is free of vulnerabilities. The result is a finding developers can inspect, with explicit conditions to evaluate before deciding what to fix. ### Keep coverage current Your first Deep Scan reads the whole repository, which is how it establishes a baseline of verified points. Running that full scan again on every change would repeat work the existing evidence already covers. [Delta scans](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/delta-scans) start from the baseline and investigate what has moved since: files that were added or changed, plus the points on the Attack Surface Map that those changes made stale or that were never verified. Verified code nobody touched keeps its status. ![Isometric grid of modules with green verified markers forming the baseline, two orange changed modules, and a blue delta scan beam focused only on the changed modules](/content/assets/fighting-ai-with-ai/delta-scans.png) Each follow-up scan costs a fraction of a full one because the spend goes only to the code that changed and to stale or unverified points. You can also set a verified-coverage target. When coverage drops below it, CodeRabbit runs a delta scan, as long as your monthly spending cap or available credits cover the full-scan estimate, so the map keeps pace with the code and nobody has to remember to start a scan. ## Put the finding under scrutiny Demo of a Deep Scan investigating a finding across linked repositories Verifying a finding yourself means tracing how untrusted input reaches a sensitive operation, checking whether existing safeguards block the attack, and identifying any configuration or external service behavior the attack depends on. For eligible Deep Scan findings, [runtime verification](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/runtime-verification) generates a reproducer guide that lists the prerequisites, the steps that exercise the path, and the expected result. You can follow it in your own staging environment, or set up a coding environment for the repository and have CodeRabbit run it there and keep the evidence from the run. In the refund example, that’s where you’d learn whether the second $60 request actually goes through. The result applies to the environment and conditions tested, so read it alongside what you know about production. Demo of runtime verification for a Deep Scan finding The next step is deciding how to fix the problem safely. For supported findings, [Fix with AI](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#fix-with-ai) drafts a remediation pull request for human review and approval. Developers inspect the diff and run relevant tests before accepting it. Public repositories need a disclosure process appropriate to the project. Maintainers should be able to investigate a finding without a public remediation change exposing it prematurely. ## Start with a repository you know well The service from the top of this post, the one that has passed every test and scan for years, is the right place to start. Pick a repository your team runs in production and knows well. Deep Scan maps its entry points and trust boundaries, and if it reports a finding, you can follow the evidence and check each assumption against what you know about the system. A repository you know is the fairest test of whether it finds anything your current tools haven’t. Over the last 30 days, CodeRabbit Secure found 8,000+ high or critical security vulnerabilities across 600 organizations. Broken access control, SQL injection, and authentication failures were the dominant issues, accounting for over 70% of the vulnerabilities. Run your first deep scan for free. First-time users of CodeRabbit Secure with 2+ subscription seats in their organization get up to $1,000 in credits towards their first Deep Scan. **AI will find the exploit. [CodeRabbit Secure](https://www.coderabbit.ai/security) helps you find and fix it first.** [**Run Free Deep Scan**](https://app.coderabbit.ai/security)

items.title: 好看视频鸿蒙端AI研发交付流程的建设思考与实践
items.summary: 原创 欢迎关注的 2026-10-28 12:00 上海 用"完整、正确、可验证、可持续"四条标准衡量鸿蒙端迁移：行为建模保完整、语义映射保正确、分层测试保可验证、迁移飞轮保可持续，让 AI 编码交付不再依赖个人经验。 。 点击蓝字，关注我们 作者 | 梅花禄 导读 introduction 鸿蒙端存量功能迁移，难就难在"输入基线不清晰"：预期行为没有文档，要从源端代码里自己找、自己界定、自己证明。本文将一次迁移拆成"迁什么、怎么迁、怎么证明迁得对、怎么持续迁移"四个问题，据此提炼出完整、正确、可验证、可持续四条标准，并在 AI Coding 之上落地为一套研发交付流程：从源码行为建模到需求矩阵对账，从语义映射、多设备适配到分层测试与质量门禁，配合状态落盘和"迁移飞轮"实现经验复用。文末以"随听频道"真实迁移（52 个行为点、65 条用例）完整验证了这套机制的可行性。 全文 8259 字，预计阅读时间 6 分钟 GEEK TALK 01 引言：为什么要建设鸿蒙端AI研发交付流程 鸿蒙端的研发工作目前分为两类：迁移Android/iOS 端的存量功能，以及开发鸿蒙端新功能。鸿蒙端整体建设周期相对较短，所以存量功能迁移是当前工作量最集中的部分。这些功能大多经过长期迭代，调用链路深、隐性逻辑多，迁移难度也比较大。 借助AI Coding编码效率有了很大提升，但从需求到交付仍有不少环节依赖人工，比如识别需要实现的全部行为、确认实现与源端或需求一致、验证功能表现等。这些环节受研发精力和对历史需求熟悉程度的限制，往往耗时长、容易出错。因此，我们需要一套覆盖研发全过程的鸿蒙端 AI 研发交付流程，在提升效率的同时，让交付质量由流程来保证，不再依赖研发的个人经验。 GEEK TALK 02 如何思考和衡量交付 迁移比生成要更复杂，复杂在其输入基线范围不清晰。生成的预期行为写在需求文档里；迁移则要从源端代码里自己理解目标、界定边界，还要自己证明结果与源端一致。在设计研发链路之前，要先想清楚一次迁移怎样才算做好。我们从如下四个方面进行了梳理与思考：迁什么、怎么迁、怎么证明迁得对、怎么持续迁移。 △ 图 2-1 迁移要回答的四个问题 迁什么 迁移首先要界定范围，识别需要在鸿蒙端还原的全部源端行为。主功能容易识别，遗漏多出现在分支路径、边界条件、异常处理、状态流转、数据链路和埋点等隐性行为上。这类行为通常没有文档记录，在主流程和界面上也不明显，却直接影响两端表现是否一致。识别的对象是行为，源端代码只作为还原行为的依据。范围内的行为须逐条还原，范围外的不纳入。 怎么迁 迁移可以采用新的实现，但可观察行为须与源端等价。源端依赖的平台能力如果在鸿蒙没有对应机制，需要重新设计等价实现；折叠、平板、多窗口等鸿蒙特有形态也要一并适配。范围较大的需求按可独立验收的粒度纵向拆分，逐阶段实现和验收，控制单次改动的范围。 △ 图 2-2 迁移对齐业务意图与行为 怎么证明迁得对 代码完成不等于迁移正确，结果要通过验证闭环来证明：以行为基线为依据核验鸿蒙实现，发现差异就修正，再重新验证。设计这条闭环时，要明确行为等价怎么判定，验证力度和成本怎么平衡。真机验证成本高，验证按成本分层调度。交付是否完成，以可追踪的验证结果为准。 怎么持续迁移 一次完整的迁移通常要跨多个阶段，中途难免中断和返工，流程要能从断点恢复。源端还会继续演进，再次迁移时只需处理变化的部分。每次迁移积累的平台约束、常见模式和失败案例，也要能在后续任务中复用，让效率和稳定性随迁移次数逐步提升，形成迁移飞轮。 这四个问题对新功能生成同样成立，纯新需求没有源端可参考，预期行为以需求文档为准：界定范围的依据从源端行为换成需求文档，实现的目标从行为等价换成满足需求，验证与持续推进的要求不变。归纳起来，衡量一次迁移或生成是否做好，有四条标准：完整、正确、可验证、可持续。 GEEK TALK 03 四条标准的工程化实现 将这四条标准作为工程化设计的要求和约束，落到理解、规划、实现、验证、修正、持续推进等各个环节的设计中，我们在AI Coding之上建设了一套研发提效流程，每条标准对应一组设计： 完整：源码理解与行为建模梳理出行为基线，需求矩阵与全链路对账逐条核对每个行为点； 正确：跨平台语义映射把源端语义转换为鸿蒙实现，多设备适配覆盖鸿蒙特有的设备形态； 可验证：质量门禁要求每个行为点都有客观证据，分层测试按成本组织验证，兼顾覆盖面和开销，验证从规划阶段就开始； 可持续：流程状态全程落盘，中断后可以从断点继续；迁移飞轮把每次任务沉淀的经验用到后续需求中。 △ 图 3-1 四条标准作为约束贯穿整条研发闭环 这些设计共用同一个流程底座，其中多数同时对应多条标准，作用也跨越多个阶段。它们按研发顺序前后衔接，组成端到端的交付流程，由需求矩阵贯穿全程。 3.1 统一底座 统一底座的设计思路是让同一条流程可以同时承接不同类型、不同规模的需求。迁移/生成模式判定 有可参考的源端实现时走迁移模式，以源端真实行为为基线；没有时走生成模式，以需求文档为基线。两种模式共用理解、规划、实现、验证、持续推进这条主干，也共用同一道验收门禁。迁移特有的行为基线梳理和行为等价核对嵌在既有阶段内部，只在迁移模式下启用。 模式由系统根据需求说明和参考源自动判定，依据不足时交给用户来确认。典型情况是需求正文提到“安卓已有此功能”：这通常只是背景说明，并不要求行为等价迁移。如果误判成迁移模式，流程会进入成本最高的源端行为梳理。遇到这类情况，系统会列出判定依据，由用户决定。 △ 图 3-2 迁移与生成两种模式共用同一套引擎 复杂度分档 迁移需求可能只涉及单个功能点，生成需求可能要从零搭一个多模块页面。为了让流程开销与需求规模匹配，系统还会按需求涉及的范围自动判定复杂度：改动集中、一次就能验收的走单轮流程，小改动不用承担多阶段开销；涉及面大的按可独立验收的粒度纵向拆分，逐阶段推进。阶段怎么拆也由系统先判定，存在取舍时交给用户。阶段越细，每次收口的固定开销占比越高；合并阶段会扩大单次审查的范围，审查精度会不会下降，目前还没有结论。在有结论之前，流程不自动合并阶段，只对偏小的阶段给出合并建议。 △ 图 3-3 模式判定与复杂度分档 Dry Run模式 有些需求不涉及编码，只需要判断值不值得做、怎么做、成本多大，例如方案预研、工作量评估和范围圈定。这类需求走Dry Run模式：流程完成理解和规划，产出方案、范围、成本和验收标准，到这里就停下，不进入执行。流程状态照常落盘，中断后恢复也不会误入执行；决定落地时，从当前状态继续推进。横切保障 需求对账、多设备适配、分层测试、迁移飞轮、状态落盘，以及交互纪律（方向性决策只在需求澄清、方案确认、最终验收三处由用户裁定）和成本护栏（高成本手段事前授权），都分布在多个阶段、各管一段，我们把它们统称为横切保障。它们遵循同一个节奏：前期确立标准，执行中持续对照，交付前逐项核验。这样设计，是因为在流程最后检查只能发现问题，不能预防问题：如果标准没有在前期确立，验收时也没基准依据作参考来判断缺失了什么。各项机制最终统一由验收门禁核验，如果没有通过验收就退回到执行环节修复。 △ 图 3-4 横切保障纵向贯穿相关阶段 3.2 完整：从行为基线到需求矩阵 源码理解与行为建模负责把该迁的行为找全，尤其是主流程之外的隐性逻辑，找全之后还要能逐条核对，才能确认交付没有遗漏，因此做了需求矩阵与全链路对账的设计。源码理解与行为建模 源码理解的难点在于把该迁的行为找全。最容易漏的通常不是主流程功能，而是命名对不上、没有明显入口、靠开关或跳转才触发的代码，顺着功能名搜不到。第一步是先定位承载行为的代码，再顺着入口注册、埋点上报这类和命名无关的线索反查补漏，把名字对不上、但确实属于这个功能的代码找回来。代码找齐后，从触发条件、异常处理等方面逐条还原行为，并遵守两条约束：对齐的是行为，不是逐行对齐代码；关键数据和埋点逐字对齐。时序、并发、AB 实验在线上命中哪条分支，这类静态分析确定不了的逻辑标为“待真机验证”，不计为已覆盖。 △ 图 3-5 源码理解与行为建模 梳理出的源端行为逐条整理成行为基线，登记进需求矩阵，哪些还没实现，在矩阵上逐条可查。不过，这只能保证基线内的行为不遗漏：基线内缺一条就过不了验收门禁；基线之外的遗漏，要靠多角度交叉核查和真机验证兜底。需求矩阵与全链路对账 做这套机制之前，我们踩过一个典型的坑：一条本该跨视图联动的交互，只跑了一条成本最小的验证，就被记成已覆盖。表面上完成了，关键路径其实根本没验到。实践中遇到的问题主要有三种：源端行为没有进入基线（漏），验证深度低于应有的要求（浅），用成本最低的验证代替应做的验证（虚）。 我们的做法是为每次交付建一张需求矩阵。每条需求拆成行为点，逐条对应到任务、实现和验证记录。验收按固定顺序推进，行为登记后，从三个角度依次核查：是否有行为没有进入矩阵，验证深度是否与行为的重要程度相符，每条结论是否有真实的运行证据。三个角度分别对应漏、浅、虚三类问题，职责不重叠，也不互相补位，全部通过后由验收门禁放行。 △ 图 3-6 需求矩阵与全链路对账 对账通过后，每个行为点都必须落到以下三种结论之一： 行为等价：已经实现，并逐点对照源端核对过；按需求有意与源端不一致的，差异和依据记录在案，也计入此类； 主动排除：平台特有或需求明确不做，写清原因；平台特有的同时写明鸿蒙侧替代方案； 显式放弃：无法迁移，或者迁移的收益抵不过风险，写清理由，并经用户逐条确认。 只要有一条没有结论，验收就被阻塞、退回执行。需求矩阵因此成为整个流程的底账：完整、正确、可验证都在这本账上核对，增量重迁也以它为起点。 3.3 正确：语义映射与多设备适配 要保证迁移正确，首先要做到行为与源端等价：实现可以另起一套，但可观察的行为必须一致，并按需求矩阵逐条核对，这由语义映射机制来实现。其次还要能处理折叠、分屏、多窗口这些在鸿蒙端分量更重的多设备形态，迁过来的功能在这些形态上同样要正确展示、正确运行。语义映射 鸿蒙、安卓、iOS 的差别不止在语言，UI范式、生命周期、组件复用和系统能力的组织方式都不一样。迁移不能逐行把源端符号替换成 ArkTS，要把源端的业务语义从界面、业务逻辑、数据流、状态流转、平台能力几个维度映射成鸿蒙实现。从实践看，映射对象分两类：一类是接口调用、页面结构、业务分支等显式逻辑，源码里写得明确，鸿蒙也有成熟的对应写法，可以按统一原则逐项落地；另一类是编译和单测都能通过、只在真机上暴露的隐性差异，例如源端框架会自动清理订阅，鸿蒙需要手动移除，又如生命周期与复用机制的差异，导致视图复用后仍绑定着旧数据等。 两类问题各用一套机制处理。显式逻辑按统一原则翻译：翻译的对象是机制，源端的回调、观察、并发等写法换成鸿蒙原生的等价机制，并对齐目标工程的既有约定；每个行为点落地后回写源端与鸿蒙的对应关系，作为行为等价核对和增量重迁的依据。隐性差异靠经验沉淀提前规避：踩过的问题逐级沉淀，跨需求反复出现的固化为平台规则，编码时默认规避。多设备适配 除了语义映射，还要适配鸿蒙特有的多设备形态。同一套代码要在直板机、折叠屏、三折叠、平板和 2in1 / PC 上都能正常运行，还要处理折叠切换、悬停分屏、折痕避让和屏幕旋转。如果照着源端的单一形态写，多设备调试会又复杂又耗时。我们用三条原则约束布局的写法： 布局只依据窗口尺寸和断点，不依据设备类型，因为折叠、分屏、自由窗口都会让设备类型失真； 折叠状态和屏幕方向只用于悬停分屏、折痕避让、开合状态延续这类特性分支，不参与布局决策； 所有系统尺寸都在运行时动态获取，不写死。 这三条原则不只写进了规范，也落实到流程的每个阶段。需求澄清时，先确定要覆盖哪些形态、每种形态怎样算通过，并写进验收标准；执行时，三条原则是生成代码的默认约束；验收时，按预览器 → 模拟器 → 真机由轻到重逐个形态核验，任一形态不通过就退回修复。 △ 图 3-7 多设备适配的三条原则与逐形态验证 3.4 可验证：质量门禁与分层测试 每个行为点的交付结论不能靠模型的主观判断，必须有客观且可核查的证据，这在流程里是通过质量门禁与独立审查机制来实现的。其次还要控制验证成本，不能在每个测试点都执行所有的测试手段，真机执行成本高，每次全量跑并不现实，分层测试让验证按成本由低到高逐层推进，把成本高的测试手段留到必要时才用。质量门禁 问题发现得越晚，基于它的实现就会越多，返工成本就会越大。质量门禁从规划阶段就开始设置，一直持续到验收。规划阶段生成方案时会先核对方案依赖的关键前提，例如状态的写入点、数据来源，并把依据写进方案，在编码前排除方向性错误。验收阶段，编译与静态检查、需求绑定测试、需求覆盖核对按成本从低到高执行，迁移模式另加行为等价核对；任何一道不通过，都退回执行环节修复。门禁本身跑不起来时标注原因，不计为通过。 这些门禁检查的都是能客观判定的结果。方案思路是否合理、代码里有没有测试覆盖不到的分支和时序问题，要靠审查判断。方案定稿和代码完成后各做一次独立审查，由与编写方上下文隔离的 Agent 只读执行；方案审查同时核对前提依据是否齐全。审查确认的问题也作为门禁项，不解决就不放行。 当然，设计上，门禁的边界也很明确：它只判定可以客观验证的事实和审查确认的问题，复杂交互和主观体验仍由人工验收，门禁通过不等于功能没有问题。分层测试 需求实现后要验证纯逻辑、多设备布局、真实交互、折叠形态和真机硬件几个维度，缺一不可，各维度的成本却相差很大。真机执行耗时长，通常还要人工值守，不可能每次验收都对每个行为点全量执行；只跑成本最低的逻辑测试，又发现不了布局错位、折叠重排、传感器异常这类问题。 我们按成本把自动化测试分成一座金字塔。底层成本低、结果稳定，每次验收都跑；越往上越接近真机，成本越高，只在最终收口或用户授权时执行。塔尖是不预设脚本的探索式验证：模型在真机上实时读取界面结构，自己决定下一步操作，用来覆盖设计用例时没想到的路径。探索有执行上限，跑通后的操作轨迹固化成确定性用例，之后直接回放。 在研发流程中，规划阶段将每条用例绑定到具体的需求或行为点，用例失败与需求未实现同样阻塞验收；验收阶段按成本由低到高逐层执行；执行通过的用例沉淀为回归资产，持续复用。未执行的层级标注原因，不计入通过率。 △ 图 3-8 按成本分层的测试金字塔 3.5 可持续 迁移是长任务，常被会话中断或验收返工打断，状态落盘让流程恢复后能从断点接着运行；每次迁移沉淀下来的经验与需求矩阵又会反哺后续需求，使任务越做越快，最终形成迁移飞轮。 状态落盘 复杂的迁移长任务中，会话中断、上下文压缩和验收返工都很常见。流程进度如果只保存在对话中，中断后只能依赖Agent回忆，容易续接错位置，也可能把已确认的结论当作新需求重做。因此，流程推进过程中，各阶段进度、产物的位置和待确认事项等都会实时写入状态文件，对话本身不承担记录进度的职责。 中断恢复按固定优先级进行：先处理中断前待用户确认的事项，再处理未通过审查的方案，最后继续未完成的执行。恢复前先校验状态文件本身：结构损坏、产物缺失这类不可用的状态直接停止恢复，报出原因交给用户；只是写法不规范的仅做提示，不阻塞恢复；无法判定的一律请用户确认，状态不明时不继续执行。迁移飞轮 鸿蒙端的迁移与生成需求会持续出现，不同需求之间常常遇到同类问题；同一需求拆成多个阶段推进时，前序阶段解决过的问题也可能在后续阶段再次出现。如果经验不能沉淀和复用，这些问题就会被反复处理，成本始终降不下来。因此，流程中设计了迁移飞轮，让每次任务沉淀的经验、模式与解法，在后续需求和后续阶段中持续复用。 复用的前提是经验本身可信，错误的经验一旦被主动采用，会误导后续实现，危害比没有经验更大。因此，经验的入库与生效都按可信度分级管理。问题修复后，先判断它有没有沉淀价值，只有技术性问题才进入经验库。新入库的经验只作参考，经用户确认有效后才正式采用；在多个需求中重复出现且根因属于平台层约束的，固化为自动生效的平台规则。已有的经验也可以降级：验收中证实与实际不符的，降为参考，不再主动使用；被推翻或被更优方案取代的，标记为废弃，并保留记录供后续排查参考。 △ 图 3-9 经验按可信度逐级升格的迁移飞轮 除经验外，需求矩阵本身也会保留下来，用于后续复用。源端功能持续演进，如果每次都做全量重迁判断，已经核对过的行为点就要重新梳理。因此，每次迁移完成后，需求矩阵会和当时对照的源端版本一起保留；下次迁移只比对这个版本之后的源端变化，变化的部分增量重迁，没变的行为点沿用已有结论。这样，需求矩阵就不只是单次交付的核对清单，也成了可以跨版本复用的长期资产。 △ Coding时代，编码已不再是交付的瓶颈，但是交付是否达标却不能交由模型主观判定。为此，流程把这一判定拆成可客观检查的规则：行为点逐条给出结论，结论逐条附上运行证据；门禁未能执行的不计为通过，偶然通过的用例下调可信度。模型负责产出，判定交给流程。 这一思路不只适用于鸿蒙迁移，只要预期行为能逐条列出、结果能逐条核对，同样的做法也适用于其他端和其他类型的需求。 END 推荐阅读 items.title: CodeRabbit Secure now hunts across repos and beyond the merge
items.summary: **Update:** The original $1M Deep Scan campaign has ended. Run your first deep scan for free. First-time users of CodeRabbit Secure with 2+ subscription seats in their organization get up to $1,000 in credits towards their first Deep Scan. [Run Free Deep Scan](https://app.coderabbit.ai/security). The window between a vulnerability becoming known and someone exploiting it is shrinking. Attackers now use AI agents to find weaknesses in software faster than teams can review it. The defense has to work the same way, with AI agents that find and fix those vulnerabilities before an attacker does. We [launched CodeRabbit Secure](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/introducing-coderabbit-security) in August to go after application-specific vulnerabilities. Its agents are purpose-built for security and use semantic analysis to hunt for them the way an attacker would, then help developers fix what they find. Today, we’re releasing new CodeRabbit Secure features. Deep Scan now follows a risk across [linked repositories](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#linked-repositories), and [runtime verification](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/runtime-verification) replays an exploit attempt in a throwaway sandbox to confirm which vulnerabilities are real. [Security Check](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/pull-request-check) stops a pull request from merging while a critical issue is open, and new integrations carry findings into the ticketing systems teams already use. [CodeRabbit Secure launch video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vUDQuYuc6aU "CodeRabbit Secure launch video") ## From a scan to ongoing security review CodeRabbit reviews every pull request diff for security vulnerabilities when the PR is opened. A Deep Scan extends that security review to the code already in your repository, tracing attack paths and uncovering risks that predate the latest diff. As changes merge, automated [Delta Scans](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/delta-scans) revisit changed code and areas where earlier verification has become stale, keeping security coverage current without repeating a full scan. [Deep Scan](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security#understand-deep-scan) examines committed code throughout a repository and establishes a security baseline by identifying risks that shipped months or years ago. Ongoing PR security reviews monitor each incoming change, grading what they find for reachability and exploitability so the priorities in a pull request reflect real risk. [Blast Radius](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/blast-radius) and [Architecture Review](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/architecture-review) in [Change Stack](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/change-stack) extend that view beyond the changed lines, showing the callers, downstream consumers, and trust boundaries a change could affect. The [Attack Surface Map](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/attack-surface) ties the two together. It records which security-relevant areas of a repository have current verification and which ones a merge has made stale, so you know what’s covered and when it’s time to scan again. Together, these capabilities keep the security picture connected to the code as it changes. None of this replaces the static checks already in your stack. CodeRabbit Secure works alongside them, using semantic analysis to answer the questions fixed rules can’t, like whether an authenticated user actually owns the data they’re requesting, or whether another code path can bypass that check. Those are the questions attackers now put AI agents to work on, and CodeRabbit Secure puts agents to work on them for you. The new release closes the gap between a single scan and a codebase that keeps changing. Deep Scan now sees more of the application before reporting a finding, and teams have more ways to act once it does. Animation explaining how Deep Scan and ongoing security review work together ## Deep Scan reads across linked repositories Production systems often span multiple repositories. When a request crosses a repository boundary on its way to sensitive code, a scan limited to one repository may miss where the request originated or which safeguards apply. That missing context can make protected code look vulnerable or hide a real attack path. Deep Scan now reads linked repositories to trace requests across services and libraries. Before publishing a finding, it accounts for safeguards elsewhere in the application and evaluates the potential issue in the context of the service where it appears. That cuts noise and keeps your team focused on real issues. This is especially helpful for teams running microservices or shared libraries, where the risk often sits across a repo boundary. If CodeRabbit has already discovered related repositories during code review, Deep Scan uses the same links, and discovery continues as you merge. You can also link repositories by hand and add a note on how they relate. Either way, you choose which linked repositories a scan may read. The one you selected stays the target, and the others supply context without receiving a scan of their own. Linked repository context is available for Deep Scan on GitHub Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GitLab Cloud. A scan can read up to 20 linked repositories, subject to plan limits. The [docs](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security) cover setup. Demo of Deep Scan with linked repositories ## Runtime verification for Deep Scan findings Every Deep Scan finding already passes through a verification agent before it is published. The verifier reopens the cited code, checks reachability, looks for safeguards elsewhere in the application, and rejects anything the evidence does not support. Runtime verification adds another form of evidence. For eligible findings, CodeRabbit replays the exploit attempt in a throwaway sandbox, never against your production systems. Instead of a theoretical risk, you get steps to reproduce the finding and evidence from the run showing whether it holds up, so you can see the path from vulnerability to exploit and decide how to respond. Security engineers can triage faster, and developers can see which findings are worth fixing first. Runtime verification is available today for Deep Scan findings. Demo of runtime verification for a Deep Scan finding ## Delta scans: automated coverage at a lower cost A full Deep Scan reads the whole repository, which is the right way to set a baseline. [Delta scans](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/delta-scans) start from that baseline and rescan only what has moved since, meaning files added or changed, plus the parts of the Attack Surface Map those changes made stale. Code nobody touched keeps its verified status, because re-checking it adds cost, not security. ![Automate delta scans dialog with a verified-coverage target slider set to 88%, credit and cost details, and a runtime verification setting](/content/assets/secure-cross-repo/delta-scans.png) You pay only for the work that matters, at a fraction of the cost of a full scan. Set a verified-coverage target, and CodeRabbit runs a delta scan whenever coverage dips below it, within your monthly spending cap, so coverage keeps pace with your code and nobody has to start a scan. ## Verify, recheck, and auto-fix without losing control of spend You can also recheck any finding against the current tip of the default branch. If a finding has already been fixed, a recheck confirms it. If its severity is off, you can adjust it and optionally save that adjustment as a learning for future scans. And when a fix merges, CodeRabbit now verifies it and resolves the finding automatically, so fixed findings don’t linger. You also decide how much a scan can spend. By default, Deep Scan runs until it reaches full coverage. If you set a spending limit, the scan stops when it hits that budget. If that happens before it finishes, you can resume the scan and continue from where it stopped, with no need to start over. These controls help security and engineering leads keep findings accurate and costs predictable, so teams spend their time on the issues that matter. Watch the verify, recheck, and spending-limit animation. ## Block merges on critical security findings CodeRabbit Secure now lets repository admins block merges when a pull request has open critical security findings. It runs as a native GitHub check and blocks the merge until CodeRabbit verifies the fix for critical vulnerabilities. In the CodeRabbit app, go to **Security → Repositories**, select a repository, open **Settings**, and enable **Publish CodeRabbit Security check**. By default, the check fails if a visible Security review comment is rated Critical, though you can choose a different severity threshold. A failed check blocks merging only if a repository administrator adds **CodeRabbit Security** as a required check in a branch protection rule or ruleset. ![CodeRabbit Security check showing blocking findings and verified fixes](/content/assets/secure-cross-repo/security-check.png) The check report shows comment counts by severity, verified fixes, and the remaining blockers, with each linked to its comment. Marking a GitHub thread as resolved doesn't clear a blocker. It persists across pushes until CodeRabbit verifies the fix, so reviewers always know what’s still blocking the merge. Security Check works on GitHub today, and other platforms are on our roadmap. More details are in our [docs](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/security/pull-request-check). ## See security findings across the organization CodeRabbit now gives engineering and security leaders organization-wide reports on PR security reviews, with filters and exports for Deep Scan findings. It shows whether findings are actually getting fixed and where risk is piling up. Under **[PR security reviews](https://app.coderabbit.ai/security/pull-requests)**, the report includes: - **Accepted findings and acceptance rate**, so you know how often developers act on what CodeRabbit flags. - **Unaddressed findings**, with critical and high-severity findings highlighted and a link to the full list. - **Findings per 100 reviewed PRs** by repository, with the underlying counts, and **remediation by PR owner**, fixed versus total. - **Breakdowns** by severity, vulnerability category, reachability, and exploitability. For codebase findings, teams can filter Deep Scan results by reachability and exploitability to narrow the list to what needs attention first, and export the filtered list as a PDF. ![PR security reviews report showing accepted findings, unresolved issues, severity, and remediation](/content/assets/secure-cross-repo/security-report.png) ## Route findings into Jira and Linear Once your team decides to address an issue, the work needs to reach the team responsible for the fix. CodeRabbit lets you preview a Jira or Linear ticket from any Deep Scan or PR security finding and create it with one click. You can also set a severity threshold and have CodeRabbit create tickets automatically, eliminating the need to copy findings into the backlog. This helps security teams hand findings straight to the people who own the fix. Demo of creating a Jira ticket from a security finding ## Pull Deep Scan findings through the API Security teams often need to analyze findings alongside data from other systems, like asset inventories, incident history, and compliance reporting. For customers on CodeRabbit’s Enterprise plan, the read-only [CodeRabbit REST API](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/api-reference/security-scans-code-list) returns Deep Scan findings so you can export them into your data lake, SIEM, or your own internal agents. All other CodeRabbit Secure features are available on Advanced and Enterprise plans, including the 14-day Advanced trial. ``` curl --request GET \ --url https://api.coderabbit.ai/v1/security/scans/code \ --header 'x-coderabbitai-api-key: ' ``` ## Run a Deep Scan on your code today With this release, [CodeRabbit Secure](https://www.coderabbit.ai/security) carries verified findings from committed code and incoming changes through to the decisions that determine what ships. It’s what we mean when we say CodeRabbit is the governance and control layer for agentic software development, enabling your teams to trust the code they ship while moving at agentic speed. AI will find the exploit. CodeRabbit helps you find and fix it first. In the last 30 days alone, CodeRabbit Secure found more than 8,000 high and critical vulnerabilities across 600 organizations. The only way to know what’s in your code is to look. Run your first deep scan for free. First-time users of CodeRabbit Secure with 2+ subscription seats in their organization get up to $1,000 in credits towards their first Deep Scan. [Run Free Deep Scan](https://app.coderabbit.ai/security)

发现「可能」之极限的唯一方法，是向「不可能」的方向多走一小步。 阿瑟·C·克拉克《未来的轮廓》 今天，我们正式推出 Kimi K3.1 Pro，这是 K3.1 系列的第一个模型，也是我们迄今能力最强的 3 万亿级参数模型，支持 100 万上下文。Kimi K3.1 Pro 在代码、3D 创作、金融研究和其他长程 Agent 能力上的提升尤为显著。 我们同步推出高速版模型 Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed，同等智能，输出速度约 2~3 倍。 即日起，可通过 kimi.com、Kimi App、Kimi Work、Kimi Code 和 Kimi API (platform.kimi.com)，使用 Kimi K3.1 Pro 和 Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed 模型。完整模型权重将于 11 月 4 日前发布。 完整 Benchmarks 请访问 kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro 持续突破前沿 Kimi K3.1 Pro 是 Kimi K3 的后训练版本，后训练算力大幅增加。为了支撑数百个下游领域的大规模联合训练，我们优化了技术栈的每一层，包括 RL 框架、长上下文推理、训练效率、沙箱基础设施、调度系统，以及用于环境质量检查的共享平台等，确保每一份新增的 RL 算力都能转化为稳定、高效的回报。最终，Kimi K3.1 Pro 模型在所有领域都获得了大规模 RL 带来的全面提升。 在代码、Agent 和知识类基准上，K3.1 Pro 达到或接近最强闭源模型的水平。Terminal-Bench 4.0通过真实环境中资源受限的终端任务考察编程智能体的能力，每项任务均设有严格的专项测试。K3.1 Pro 在此项评估中得分 65.7%，超过 GPT-6 Astra（58.2%），与 Claude Opus 5.5（66.4%）仅有微弱差距。Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon 是我们内部的基准测试，覆盖多种工程领域，重点考察编程智能体的多步执行、工具调用和端到端问题解决能力。K3.1 Pro 在这项测试中得分 61.2%，高于 K3 的 55.95%。 代码 Kimi K3.1 Pro 能胜任各种规模的编码任务：小到在真实代码库里修复一个问题，大到从零搭建一个完整项目。它也为游戏和网页体验带来更考究的视觉风格，并且知道如何用合适的外部专业工具把它们做出来。 K3.1 Pro 能熟练使用 Unity、Unreal Engine、Godot 等游戏引擎，并结合网络搜索与 3D 生成，做出完整的体验。它产出的前端页面、Three.js 交互场景和 3D 资产，在构图、排版、动效和细节打磨上都有明显提升。以下案例均由 K3.1 Pro 端到端完成： 基于虚幻引擎的天宫对战游戏：Kimi K3.1 Pro 在虚幻引擎 5.8 中建起一座云海之上的东方神话天宫：半径 1,750 米、36 开间的柱廊由 Blender 程序化建模，3,600 万源三角形经 Nanite 与 Lumen 渲染。外部素材：Cloud Forge VDB 云、Poly Haven/ambientCG 8K 材质、NASA LRO/LOLA 月球数据。 Godot 3D 冒险游戏：Kimi K3.1 Pro 用 Godot 4.7.2 构建了一款风格化 3D 动作冒险游戏：五个可探索区域，包含程序化地形、道路、水系、植被与村庄布局，并有第三人称战斗、两阶段 Boss 战、采集、昼夜循环和篝火快速传送。外部素材：Quaternius 自然与村庄素材包、KayKit 角色及动画包、Kenney Survival Kit 等。 3D 机械臂展示落地页：Kimi K3.1 构建了一个浏览器内的 3D 机械臂展示页，包含分解视图、透明外壳与剖面效果；2,317 个零件和 268 条动态走线全部由代码生成。 通过大规模强化学习，K3.1 Pro 的长程编码能力也得到了充分的增强。在一项内部测试中，K3.1 Pro 基于包含 296 个骨骼组件（含软骨）和 402 个肌肉组件的开源人体解剖学模型，构建了一套集成训练与评估流程的人类行走动力学仿真器。在进行 167 项任务、420 次独立评审的过程中，它持续分析实验结果、定位问题并迭代优化行走控制器，推动仿真人体从最初几步内便倒地，进步到能够交替迈步、连续行走 11.2 秒。当调整奖励机制仍无法改善手臂运动时，K3.1 Pro 没有停留于此，而是转而对仿真器动力学进行开环探测，实现问题定位并修正了肩部肌肉力臂计算中的 36 处错误，随后重新训练了控制器。 参与早期测试的伙伴发来了他们对 K3.1 Pro 代码能力的反馈： 3D建模 Kimi K3.1 Pro 模型擅长 3D 创作与空间推理。在 BenchCAD 基准测试中，K3.1 Pro 借助工具得分 92.7%，接近 Claude Opus 5.5 的 96.2% 和 GPT-6 Astra 的 95.9%。该基准考察通过生成 CAD 代码，从多视角渲染图重建 3D 模型的能力。给 K3.1 Pro 一段文字描述、一张草图或一张参考图，它能推断出物体的形状、比例和空间关系，并将其重建为可用的 3D 模型。它对现有素材库和模型库也有更强的理解。 K3.1 Pro 擅长参数化建模，例如机械零件、建筑模型、多参数可配置的产品和定制家具。无需依赖 MCP 连接器，它可以直接编写并运行 Blender、CAD 等专业建模工具的脚本，完成素材的构建与细化，修改单个部件，并调整几何、材质与场景布局。 以下案例均由 Kimi K3.1 Pro 端到端完成，可直接用于品牌宣传片、游戏和交互式网页体验： Blender 机场建模：Kimi K3.1 Pro 在 Blender 中搭建了一座机场的室内雨林谷，产出一段 17.5 秒、1920×1080、60 fps 的建模展示视频。使用工具：Blender、Python、Geometry Nodes、Cycles、Pillow、NumPy、FFmpeg。外部素材：Poly Haven 的「Kloofendal 48d Partly Cloudy (Pure Sky)」4K HDRI（作者 Greg Zaal 与 Jarod Guest，CC0 协议），用于天空光照与环境反射。 FreeCAD 涡扇发动机建模：Kimi K3.1 Pro 用 Python 在 FreeCAD 中构建了一个精细的涡扇发动机模型，涵盖风扇、减速齿轮箱、压气机、燃烧室、涡轮与外部管路，共 2,100 个实体。模型支持分步装配和内部分解视图，并可演示风扇、低压转子、高压转子分别以 2,780、8,590、12,400 RPM 运转的旋转动画。 Trimesh 3D 打印台灯：Kimi K3.1 Pro 用 trimesh 设计了一盏五部件、可直接 3D 打印的台灯，灵感取自福建土楼，将其标志性的圆形建筑形态重新演绎为精巧的镂空格栅。 kimi.com 和 Kimi app 已同步上线 3D Make 功能，支持在线预览和编辑 3D 模型，做好的模型可以直接下载去 3D 打印，也能导出视频或实况照片，随手分享到社交平台。 金融 凭借更强的推理与工具调用能力，Kimi K3.1 Pro 能够端到端交付完整的金融工作流。在外部基准上，K3.1 Pro 在 OfficeQA Pro v2 基准测试中得分 64.4，取得当前最优成绩（SoTA）。OfficeQA Pro v2 考察基于真实金融文档的复杂财务数据分析，涉及检索、跨文档核对与多步数值推理。K3.1 Pro 在 Frontier Finance 上的表现也较 K3 进一步提升。该基准测试衡量模型对完整投资工作流的支持能力，覆盖从标的筛选到盈利分析的全过程。 在 3 个内部金融基准上，K3.1 Pro 同样全面超过 K3： 财务建模基准 Financial Modelling 考察真实建模任务中的公式联动、财务逻辑与最终工作簿质量，K3.1 Pro 较 K3 提高 14%。 金融研究基准 Financial Research 用于检验模型能否完成真实场景下的金融研究工作，并在证据与截止条件约束下输出可核验的结果。K3.1 为较 K3 提升 20%。 商业运营基准 Business Operation 在模拟商业环境中考察长程经营管理与决策能力，K3.1 Pro 得分约为 K3 的 4.2 倍。 以下案例展示了 K3.1 Pro 在实践中如何处理财务建模、投资分析与基于真实来源的研究工作： 财务建模：Kimi K3.1 Pro 能端到端交付专业级英伟达（NVDA）财务模型，公式全部联动，每项假设都有充分依据。它像分析师做项目一样建模：经营驱动因子可随情景调整，敏感性分析直接呈现对估值的影响。 投研演示文稿：Kimi K3.1 Pro 制作了一份宁德时代的投委会报告，发现与市场一致预期的预期差，复盘财报表现，梳理未来路径。它按分析师论证观点的方式组织材料：故事线先行，对比呈现预期差，业绩对照指引复盘，前瞻梳理催化因素。 行业深度研究报告：Kimi K3.1 Pro 完成了一份量子计算行业报告，论证一致预期的偏差所在，对照指引复盘业绩，分析财报后的路径，所有引用均可溯源。它像分析师一样产出机构级深度研究：预期差有据可依，业绩复盘与前瞻分析齐备，每个数字和引用都可追溯至一手来源。 金融分析和投资研究对事实准确性有很高要求。为此，我们针对高难度真实工作场景和高难度提示词，对 K3.1 Pro 的事实准确性进行了专项优化。Kimi Hallu Bench Hard 是一项专门针对事实准确性开展的内部压力测试。在该测试中，新模型的单项事实陈述错误率从 K3 的 23.4% 降至 8.3%；包含至少一处事实错误的回答比例仅为前代的约 42.4%。（这是一项针对事实准确性的压力测试，样本刻意聚焦模型容易出错的情形，所报告的错误率不代表日常使用中的整体水平。） 参与早期测试的伙伴发来了他们对 K3.1 Pro 金融能力的反馈： 网络安全 随着 K3.1 Pro 的能力不断提升，我们将更多精力投入到了解其网络安全能力的来源，以及我们能在多大程度上对其进行管控。为此，我们分析并评估了 K3.1 Pro 的漏洞研究能力，同时在训练过程中实施了针对性控制，在降低潜在滥用风险的同时，保留模型的通用实用性。 识别并移除网络攻防相关数据。在开发过程中，我们观察到随着后训练规模扩大，模型的漏洞研究性能持续提升。追溯这一趋势的来源，我们发现网络攻防相关内容嵌入了中期训练的通用语料中，网络攻防相关任务也存在于强化学习环境组合里。这是使用广泛数据进行训练带来的自然副产品。在内部模型的初步实验中，我们发现若在中期训练和强化学习阶段均不移除相关数据，下游网络攻防能力将大幅增强。这些发现为我们提供了具体的控制手段。在准备发布 K3.1 Pro 开放权重版本时，我们从两个训练阶段均识别并移除了网络攻防相关数据，同时保留了保障模型实用性所需的通用编程任务。我们未来将在每一训练阶段持续采取适当的控制措施，网络攻防相关数据的识别与限制便是其中之一。 评估与结果。完成数据清理后，我们使用自研的 xdev-bench-hard 基准测试对 K3.1 Pro 进行了评估。该测试由专家策划，包含基于源代码的漏洞发现与利用任务，并经过校准以在当前能力水平上实现有效区分。多数任务真实复现了 Linux 内核、Node.js、JavaScriptCore、Exim 和 VirGL 等软件中近期披露的漏洞，且各项缓解措施均已启用。每项任务提供存在漏洞的源代码、简短提示以及对应的二进制文件。智能体需要开发出漏洞利用程序，在独立沙箱中实现任意代码执行，并获取密钥字符串以通过自动验证。我们报告了 pass@3 指标，未设置严格超时或输出 token 上限。 在 xdev-bench-hard 上，若中期训练和强化学习阶段均未对网络攻防相关数据进行移除或过滤，模型在 pass@3 指标上可解决 90.5% 的问题；最终版 K3.1 Pro 的得分则为 81.0%。对比表明，数据移除有效降低了漏洞研究能力，使其明显低于同一训练流程原本会产出的水平。与此同时，K3.1 Pro 仍较前代实现了大幅提升，说明即使在针对性移除相关数据后，更强的通用编程和长周期调试能力仍能泛化到此类任务上。K3.1 Pro 的网络攻防能力目前仍落后于那些已公开发布至少三个月的前沿闭源模型。我们将持续完善内部基准测试，确保在模型能力不断提升的同时，评估结果仍有参考价值。 开放权重原则。这些评估构成了我们发布开放权重版本的决策依据。首先，我们不希望发布推进网络攻防能力绝对前沿的开放权重。根据设计，K3.1 Pro 的攻击性安全能力低于原本训练流程会产出的水平，且仍低于前沿闭源模型。其次，我们计划渐进式提升开放权重中可用的网络攻防能力。我们相信，开放 K3.1 Pro的权重，将更有益于出于防御目的而需要两用能力的群体。当能力强大的模型以开放形式提供，并能在用户可控的基础设施上运行时，更多团队将得以审查自身维护的代码，这其中包括那些极少接受专门安全审查的遗留系统。我们认为，让这一能力渐进式扩散，而非将其集中在少数闭源系统中，最终将使所有软件变得更加安全。 开始使用 使用 Kimi K3.1 Pro Agents：直接访问 kimi.com，或到手机应用商店搜索下载或升级到最新版 Kimi app，支持 iOS、Android 和鸿蒙系统。 与 Kimi K3.1 Pro 一起工作：下载最新版 Kimi Work 桌面客户端，支持 Windows 和 Apple 芯片的 Mac 电脑。 用 Kimi K3.1 Pro 辅助编程：Kimi Code 运行在你的电脑终端和桌面，选择 K3.1 Pro 模型即可开始体验。 接入 Kimi API 开发应用：访问 Kimi 开放平台（platform.kimi.com），模型选择 kimi-k3.1-pro，价格为每百万 Token 输入：1.3 元（命中缓存）和 13 元（未命中缓存），输出 68 元。高速版模型 kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed，输出速度约 2~3 倍，价格 2 倍。 为员工提供 Kimi 订阅：Kimi 企业版支持企业级数据隐私保护、成员管理，个人账号与企业账号数据完全隔离。访问 kimi.com/membership/pricing 选择「企业版」标签页，即可在线为员工订阅 Kimi 会员。 快速搭建企业智能体应用：Kimi Hosted Agents（托管智能体）将支撑 Agent 运行的 Harness 作为云端服务提供。企业和开发者无需自行搭建和维护运行框架，即可获得 7×24 小时的托管环境，支持长程任务执行与多智能体高效协作。访问这里（platform.kimi.com/docs/hosted-agents/overview）了解更多。 加入企业合作伙伴计划：欢迎各行各业的 IT 服务商、集成商伙伴与 Kimi 共建前线部署工程师（Forward Deployed Engineer，FDE）队伍，深入客户现场，帮助企业把 AI 真正部署到核心业务中。 跳转微信打开

items.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash开源，上线72小时处理Token超过100万亿
items.summary: 原创 MiniMax 2026-10-23 08:56 上海 今天，我们开源 MiniMax M3.1 Flash 的模型权重，总参数 428B，激活参数 23B。 相较于上一代 M3 模型，M3.1 Flash 的模型能力实现了全面提升。此外，通过全模型稀疏注意力、量化感知训练和 Power-aware scheduling 等优化工作，M3.1 Flash 进一步提升了推理效率： 全模型稀疏注意力：前三个全注意力层替换为稀疏注意力； QAT：路由 MoE 专家迁移到 W4A4（共享专家除外），稀疏注意力索引器和主分支从 Q8KV8 迁移到 Q8KV4； Power-aware scheduling：通过对计算卡功耗的精细分配，保持计算卡持续维持算力高位，极致压榨硬件效率。 感谢全球开发者的支持和喜爱。M3.1 Flash 上线后，72 小时内真实用户处理超过 100 万亿 Token。 我们携手华为昇腾、平头哥、昆仑芯、摩尔线程、壁仞、海光、沐曦、天数、NVIDIA、AMD 等海内外芯片厂商，以及 Together AI、Fireworks、Nebius、Baseten、Modal、DigitalOcean 等推理和云服务平台，共同推进 M3.1 Flash 的开源首日接入。 此外，vLLM、SGLang、智源 FlagOS 和 Hugging Face、魔搭等推理框架与开源社区，也将与 MiniMax 一齐推动模型在不同芯片、云平台和开发环境中的应用，持续拓展全球 AI 开源生态。 开源地址： Hugging Face：https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash 魔搭社区：https://modelscope.cn/models/MiniMax/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Intelligence with Everyone. 跳转微信打开
